persona.who: 22, wants to be a filmmaker, father is a government doctor who wants him to do MBBS or at least MBA. Fights every dinner.
persona.note: papa says films are for rich kids and I should do MBA. we fight every night. I love him and I also feel like he doesn't see me at all. mummy cries in the kitchen

understanding.bridge: The fight every night is what happens when your worth is made to depend on your father's praise. The Gita calls it a mind that cannot stand on its own.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the fight and the ache, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the battlefield is your need for his approval, and that it keeps the mind unsteady.
week_beats.steady: You hold that your truth is not his to give or take.
week_beats.act: You try saying the true thing once, calmly, and then do what you can to study films.
week_beats.story: A son who stood in his truth and a father who slowly learned to see him shows you what standing on your own ground looks like.

understanding.core_struggle: A student under twenty-five wants to study films but her father dismisses it and they fight every night, while her mother cries in the kitchen.
understanding.mirror: You love films and want to study them, and every night you fight for it while your mother cries in the kitchen.
understanding.insight: It isn't the MBA he wants for you. It's that he cannot yet see the life you are reaching for, and you are caught between his worry and your own truth.

queries.hook: Wanting to study what you love while the person you love cannot see it, and the ache of fighting for it every single night. I keep fighting with my parents.
queries.diagnose: When your worth depends on another's praise, every word of blame shakes you; craving approval keeps the mind unsteady and turns love into a battlefield.
queries.steady: Praise and blame come and go, but the truth of what you are is not theirs to give or take; stand on your own ground and let the storm pass.
queries.act: Practise saying the true thing to him, calmly and once; then do what you can to study films, and let his reaction be his.
queries.story: A son who wanted to be an artist and a father who could only see security, where the son stood in his truth and the father slowly learned to see him.

weeks: The truth he cannot yet see

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयोयद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः । यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषामस्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः ॥
verse.line: I can't tell which is better, or even what winning would look like.
verse.translation: Nor do we know which is better for us, to fight or not, or whether we will win or they will. The very people after whose death we would not wish to live stand facing us.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is on the battlefield, and they are weeping. They cannot tell which choice is better, whether fighting or not fighting, or who will win. The people they would not want to outlive are standing before them. They admit they do not know what to do and ask for guidance.
verse.for_you: The fight each night is not about films or grades. It is about standing in a place where you do not know which choice is better. You do not need to win the argument. You only need to admit that you are confused and ask for help.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on wealth: a satire on how money buys reputation.
verse.sanskrit: यस्यास्ति वित्तं स नरः कुलीनः स पण्डितः स श्रुतवान् गुणज्ञः । स एव वक्ता स च दर्शनीयः सर्वे गुणाः काञ्चनमाश्रयन्ति ॥
verse.line: Have money and suddenly you are wise, well-born and charming. All virtues seem to lodge in gold.
verse.translation: Whoever has wealth is well-born, learned, well-read and a judge of merit; he is the eloquent one, the handsome one. All virtues take shelter in gold.
verse.why: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.
verse.misuse: Satire on the world's flattery, not advice to chase money.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari writes that whoever has wealth is suddenly seen as wise, well-born, and charming. All virtues seem to live in gold. He is showing how the world changes its view of a person based on money, not on who they actually are.
verse.for_you: Your father sees only the life he fears for you. He does not yet see the person you are becoming. His worry is not your truth, and his doubt is not your worth.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
verse.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
verse.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: In the Niti Shatakam, Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from a place of quiet certainty. He has seen how quickly the world changes its mind and how unstable its rewards are. He tells us to let the crowd praise or blame, to let money come or go, and to accept that life can end at any moment. His point is simple. The person who is steady does not step off the right path. They keep going no matter what happens outside them.
verse.for_you: You are holding your truth while your father shouts. Let the fight happen. Let him praise or blame. Your worth is in the work you do, not in his words. Keep going to your classes. Let his noise stay outside the door.

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: न हृष्यत्यात्मसंमाने नावमानेन तप्यते / गाङ्गो ह्रद इवाक्षोभ्यो यः स पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Don't swell with praise or burn at a slight; stay deep and still like a river pool.
verse.translation: One who is not elated when honoured, nor pained when slighted, and who stays unruffled like a deep pool of the Ganga, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.meaning: Vidura speaks to the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before a great war. The king is anxious and caught in the middle of his sons' greed and his own weakness. Vidura tells him to stop letting praise make him swell and insults make him burn. He says a wise person stays deep and still like a river pool. They do not get shaken by what other people say.
verse.for_you: When your father dismisses your films, do not burn. Let his words pass over you like wind. Stay deep and still. Your path is your own. Keep your focus on your studies and your own knowing.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Yudhishthira
verse.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
verse.sanskrit: आत्मानं च परांश्चैव त्रायते महतो भयात् / क्रुध्यन्तमप्रतिक्रुध्यन्दूयोरेष चिकित्सकः
verse.line: Don't answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people, and heals both.
verse.translation: One who does not get angry back at an angry person saves both himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both.
verse.why: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.misuse: Staying calm is not the same as staying in a situation where you are unsafe.

prasang.title: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.story_hook: Thirteen years into exile, Draupadi looked at her husband and asked why he was not angry.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

verse.meaning: In the forest, after their kingdom is lost, Draupadi asks Yudhishthira why he forgives their enemies instead of fighting back. He answers that answering anger with anger only destroys both sides. He says the one who stays calm saves himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both. The verse proposes that anger rarely fixes anything, and wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.for_you: The kitchen crying and the shouting are not your worth. You can say the true thing once, calmly, and then step back. Let the evening belong to your film notes.

verse.speaker: Narada (quoted by Bhishma)
verse.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse.sanskrit: ज्ञातीनां वक्तुकामानां कटुकानि लघूनि च / गिरा त्वं हृदयं वाचं शमयस्व मनांसि च
verse.line: When relatives are about to say something bitter, calm things down with your own gentle words.
verse.translation: When relatives are about to say bitter or petty things, calm their hearts, their words and their minds with your own words.
verse.why: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

prasang.title: Krishna's family troubles: the weapon not made of iron
prasang.summary: Even Krishna struggles with his clan: he does their work, bears their harsh words, and feels like the mother of two gamblers playing each other. Narada tells him the only weapon that works is soft: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
prasang.story_hook: Krishna, who guided a war, admitted to a sage that he could not keep the peace in his own family.
prasang.lesson: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells the sage Narada about his own family feuds and asks how to keep the peace. Narada replies that when relatives are about to say something bitter, you calm their hearts and minds with your own gentle words. The verse proposes that in family trouble, the only weapon that works is softness: patience, respect and gentle speech.
verse.for_you: Your father's words may come hard again. Meet them with a calm sentence, not a fight. Then turn back to your screen and your film.

story.title: Father and son go back to school
story.story_hook: When his son came home stumped, Uddalaka did something unusual for a famous teacher.
story.summary: A patron asks young Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer. He asks his father, who admits he does not know either and suggests they both go to the patron as students. Chitra welcomes Uddalaka for his humility.
story.lesson: A parent who says 'let's learn together' teaches more than any answer.

anchor.speaker: Shvetaketu and Uddalaka Aruni
anchor.setting: A patron asks Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer; he goes to his father.
anchor.sanskrit: स होवाच नाहमेतद्वेद हन्ताचार्यं प्रच्छानीति स ह पितरमासाद्य पप्रच्छेतीति स होवाचाहमप्येतन्न वेद सदस्येव वयं स्वाध्यायमधीत्य हरामहे यन्नः परे ददत्येह्युभौ गमिष्याव इति ॥
anchor.line: 'I don't know either,' the father told his son. 'Let's both go and learn, as students.'
anchor.translation: He said, 'I do not know this. Let me ask my teacher.' He went to his father and asked. The father said, 'I too do not know it. We have studied the Veda and take what others give us. Come, let us both go.'
anchor.why: A parent who says 'let's learn together' teaches more than any answer.

script: You are carrying a fight every night and a silence in the kitchen. You feel torn and unseen, caught between the life you want and the one your father wants for you. It is exhausting to be pulled apart like this.

Arjuna stands on a battlefield, and he is weeping. He looks at the people he loves and cannot tell if fighting is right or wrong. He does not know who will win, and he does not know which choice is better. And Arjuna said:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयोयद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः, यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषामस्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः.
In plain words: I can't tell which is better, or even what winning would look like.

He admits he is confused. He cannot see the path forward, and he asks for help. This is where clarity begins. It is not a sign of weakness to not know what to do. It is an honest admission that the mind is caught between two truths and needs a guide.

When your father speaks tonight, you do not have to win the argument. You can name that you do not know which choice is better. You can ask for help in finding your own way, without asking him to change.
What would it feel like to let yourself not know?

depth.life: You sit in your room at night, scrolling through films and feeling the weight of the fight downstairs. Your father's voice is loud in your head, and you feel unseen. You want to study films, but you cannot tell if that is the right path, or if you are just fighting for pride.
depth.points: Arjuna stood on the battlefield and admitted he did not know which was better, to fight or not to fight. Your mind is in that same place. You are not sure if choosing films or choosing your father's path is better. The truth is that you cannot see the whole picture right now.
depth.practice: Put the phone down and sit with that confusion for one minute without trying to fix it or judge it.
depth.question: What would it feel like to tell your father you do not know which path is right?
